doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: From jazz snob to every kind of gig
summary: Marini recalls playing with Les Elgart, backing Homer & Jethro and Flatt & Scruggs, which ended his jazz snobbery; he describes the genre-switching challenge of New York jingles.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You know when I was in school at North Texas State I was a jazz snob. And then I was playing with Les Elgart’s band and we had a gig up in — Les used to pick up, as did many bands — would pick up horn sections from North Texas. So we were playing with all kinds of — I mean I played the Lipizzaner Stallions, I played the Fort Worth Rodeo, I played the little military base gigs in the officers’ club, I mean every possible gig you can imagine. Ice shows, Stevie Wonder, Gladys Knight & the Pips, you know we ran the gamut. We played for so many people. But I remember Flatt & Scruggs. Well the first thing that happened, we had to back up Homer & Jethro and after we rehearsed with them, and they were great, you know they were funny as hell. And after we rehearsed with them we started a little jam session and I don’t remember which of them was the mandolin player, whether it was Homer or Jethro, but whichever one he was, he sat in with us and he played better than any of us. And then that night Flatt & Scruggs, the bluegrass guys, were the opening act. And I think we were playing for dancing or something. And Flatt & Scruggs, their first tune was a blistering uptempo [scats] bluegrass. And they were so relaxed and just played their asses off. And I think that was the point that my jazz snobbery went out the window. And so one reason that my sort of © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

history is so broad is that I like all kinds of music and the challenge of fitting in and trying to be yourself and play something pure and still honor the genre and not go outside of it, which I always thought was a great challenge. That was one of the things about the years in the jingles in New York. You know at ten o’clock in the morning you’re playing flutes with like a Mozart style classical ensemble, and an hour later you’re playing a New Orleans style funk tenor solo on a jingle you know. And I always loved that, and the challenge of that, and the pride and the cadre of musicians I was playing with in New York at that time. I mean you know we would be on sessions and the saxophones would be Mike Brecker and Ronnie Cuber and Dave Sanborn and myself. So you know you’re on your toes. Are you really supposed to be here with these monsters? And so that is a reason why, and I still feel that way, to challenge yourself to try to honor whatever genre you’re playing in.
